title: The naive framing: "it's a git task, right?"
text: Someone assumed submitting a workshop solution is just a Git task, commit, push, open a PR. It isn't quite, so is submitting a solution actually a feedback task? A skill is a folder

title: Anatomy: five steps, fixed order
text: Claude reads before it acts. This one is submit solution for a workshop attendee wrapping up the stock pilot exercise. Inside are five steps always in this order. Ask about their experience, show the diff, commit and push, open the PR, confirm. The skill MD fixes that order. Claude doesn't skip ahead to committing.

title: Mechanism: three questions, then git
text: Step one comes before any Git command and three questions. Which sub-agent approach did they use for cycle three? Callable agent, spawn sub-agent, inline, or something else? What was the hardest part of the workshop? One thing they'd change. Only after that does Claude check the diff. An empty diff doesn't mean they're finished. It usually means they edited a different file, so Claude asks rather than assumes. A full diff doesn't mean the PR opens yet either. The feedback still has to be collected first. title: The PR body has two sections: code summary and feedback
text: Two things in one document. The technical summary, sub-agent approach, eval score, tools dropped, skills enabled, and the workshop feedback right below it. That's what makes this a feedback task wearing a Git task's clothes. The same PR facilitators read for the code is the form they read for what to fix in the next workshop. Skip the questions and the commit still happens, but the second half of that document stays blank every time.

title: Carry-out
text: Submitting a workshop solution isn't just a Git task. The skill has Claude ask what was hardest before it commits anything because the same PR that shows the code is the form that shapes the next workshop. Your turn. Paste this

title: Your turn
text: Into Claude. I just finished a coding exercise and want to submit my solution as a pull request. Before you touch Git, ask me what approach I used, what was hardest, and what I'd change. Then show me the diff and write a PR description with two sections, my code summary and my feedback. Notice which questions come before the commit and which come after. Feedback before the commits. Lay 'em in
